questions.q: Why is WEP considered broken and deprecated?
options: It reused a small set of encryption keys in a way that let attackers mathematically recover the key from captured traffic, often in minutes
It never actually encrypted any traffic at all
It was replaced before it was ever used in any real network
It only worked on 5GHz Wi-Fi bands
questions.explain: WEP's key reuse leaked enough patterns that attackers with modest captured traffic and common tools could recover the key quickly.

questions.q: What does the WPA2 4-way handshake accomplish?
options: It confirms the access point and device derived the same session key from the password, without sending that key over the air
It permanently disables encryption after the first connection
It broadcasts the Wi-Fi password in plaintext to speed up connections
It only runs once per access point, never once per device
questions.explain: The four messages let both sides confirm they hold a matching session key derived from the shared password, without transmitting the key itself.

questions.q: What is WPA2's best-known weak point, and how does WPA3 address it?
options: A captured 4-way handshake enables offline dictionary attacks; WPA3's SAE handshake resists that style of attack
WPA2 has no known weaknesses, and WPA3 was created for unrelated reasons
WPA2 cannot encrypt any traffic, and WPA3 fixes that by removing encryption entirely
WPA2's weakness is physical range, which WPA3 fixes with stronger antennas
questions.explain: WPA3 replaces the password exchange with SAE (the dragonfly handshake), which is specifically designed to resist offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake.

questions.q: Why is open Wi-Fi (no password) considered dangerous, even if a user only visits HTTPS sites on it?
options: The network itself has no encryption between device and access point, so anyone else on it can potentially observe other unencrypted traffic
HTTPS sites cannot be loaded at all on open Wi-Fi
Open Wi-Fi networks are always evil twins by definition
Open Wi-Fi uses WPA3 encryption automatically
questions.explain: Open networks have zero network-level encryption; HTTPS protects individual connection content, but the surrounding network offers no protection of its own.

questions.q: What makes an evil-twin attack effective against most victims?
options: The fake access point broadcasts the same network name as the real one, and most people have no reliable way to tell the two apart
It requires the victim to manually install malicious software first
It only works on networks that use WPA3 encryption
It physically disconnects the real access point from the internet
questions.explain: An evil twin impersonates a legitimate SSID; since devices and people usually can't distinguish two networks with the identical name, victims connect to the fake one unknowingly.
